title: Diwali Home Décor Guide: Candles, Tableware and Pieces Worth Making Room For
excerpt: Harper's Bazaar India's 13-piece Diwali edit — from a ₹29,000 Lladró candle to a ₹2,500 photo frame — layered over the classic formula of diyas, rangoli, marigolds and warm light.
body:
• Harper's Bazaar India's Diwali décor edit is built around 13 statement pieces — candles, serveware, cushions and sculpture — rather than a full-room overhaul.
  • Standout picks include the Lladró North Tower Candle 1001 Lights at ₹29,000, a Collektklove Ganesh sculpture at ₹35,500, and Seva Home x Payal Singhal's tuberose scented candle at ₹3,995.
  • The practical layer underneath is classic: diyas clustered in odd numbers, a rangoli at the entrance, marigold garlands and lighting layered at different heights.
  • Start with the entrance and living room — the two spaces guests see first — and keep table centres low so people can see each other across the food.

An edit built on statement pieces, not a shopping spree

The most useful idea in Harper's Bazaar India's festive décor edit is restraint. Its 13 picks are objects that earn their place on a shelf or table all season: a sculptural candle, a set of dinner plates with Devanagari lettering, brass cocktail glasses, a tapestry cushion cover. Nothing on the list needs a room redesigned around it.

At the top end, the Lladró North Tower Candle 1001 Lights (₹29,000) and the Collektklove Ganesh sculpture (₹35,500) are the two investment pieces — one for light, one for the puja corner or console. In the middle sit the entertaining pieces a Diwali host actually uses repeatedly: Mérci's Devanagari assorted dinner plates, a set of four for ₹12,000; Shivan & Narresh Iconomash snack platters at ₹11,950; Baarique's Chameli Pital cocktail glasses, a set of two for ₹7,475; and Good Earth's Jaipur Rose Guldasta serving tray at ₹5,500.

Light first: candles, tapers and diyas

Diwali décor starts with light, and the edit leans into it at several price points. The Seva Home x Payal Singhal scented candle in tuberose (₹3,995) pairs fragrance with a decorative vessel, while Pottery Barn's ornate hand-painted taper holder (₹5,500) gives tall candles a proper festive base. Layer those with the oldest tools in the festival: clay diyas.

According to Square Yards' Diwali decoration guide, clustering diyas in odd numbers — three, five, seven — along windowsills, staircases and entrance paths creates a more layered look than spacing them evenly, and floating diyas in a wide brass or ceramic urli with water and flower petals make an easy coffee-table centrepiece. The same guide advises planning lighting in layers — warm string lights along walls and window frames as the base, lanterns at varied heights, and diyas low down — rather than relying on one bright overhead light. LED options, it notes, use less electricity and produce less heat.

Dress the table and the sofa

Textiles and tableware do the quiet work. The Oma Tree Tapestry cushion cover (₹6,995) changes a sofa's whole register for the price of one cover, and the Plate & Peonie green and white temple jar (₹5,700) works as a vase or a standalone object. For the table itself, Atola Papers' Bobbles tumbler in green (₹5,250) adds colour without another serving set to store.

Square Yards makes the same point from the practical side: a festive table runner, coordinated serveware and a small floral centrepiece with tea lights will carry a family dinner, and the centre should stay low so guests can see each other. Personal pieces finish the room — the Nicobar Tropics gift set of three mini photo frames (₹4,500) and Amala Earth's Bloom Frame (₹2,500) are the edit's reminder that family photographs are décor too, especially at a festival built around gathering.

The entrance, the rangoli and the puja corner

Before any statement piece matters, the basics have to be in place. A rangoli at the main entrance — powder, flower petals or a reusable mat — is the traditional welcome, and marigold garlands along the door frame remain the fastest way to make a doorway read as festive. In the puja space, the Square Yards guide suggests cleaning the mandir first, then rebuilding it with fresh flower garlands, small mats for the Lakshmi and Ganesha idols, and a ring of small diyas or tea lights rather than a single large lamp, kept bright but soft.

For diaspora homes — apartments and rentals where open flames are a problem — the formula scales down cleanly: LED tea lights, a petal rangoli or reusable mat that leaves no powder in the carpet, and one or two durable pieces that come back out every year.

What to buy, what to skip

The pattern across both guides is consistent: spend on light and on the table, where guests gather, and let everything else be flowers, textiles and things you already own. A cleaned, warmly lit home dressed at the entrance reads as Diwali-ready with three new pieces — or none.
